question: Can data-driven scheduling reduce student waiting time and improve faculty-student meeting efficiency compared with the current/manual scheduling approach?

config.tuning_note: Intelligent weights were hand-tuned on the tuning seeds (medium load) only; evaluation seeds were never used for tuning.

fcfs.label: FCFS / manual
fcfs.description: Fixed 15-minute posted slots, first come first served, class timetable ignored until a clash is found (counted as a conflict), no waiting list.

rule_based.label: Rule-based
rule_based.description: Every 30 min: sort by priority, then earliest-fit slot that respects the class timetable and the student's window. No waiting list.

intelligent.label: Intelligent (proposed)
intelligent.description: Explainable scoring: priority + fairness aging + window slack + no-show risk decide who goes first; wait + packing + peak spreading decide where; waiting-list back-fill and urgent displacement recover lost capacity.

avg_wait_incl_unserved_min.label: Avg wait incl. unserved (charged full window)

conclusions: Waiting time: intelligent 219 min vs FCFS 246 min (10.8% lower, better) and vs rule-based 215 min (1.9% higher, worse).
Meetings held: 175 vs 161 (FCFS) and 174 (rule-based); success rate 73.0% vs 66.9% and 72.4%.
Faculty time: idle time 4082 min vs 4340 (FCFS) / 4106 (rule-based); schedule conflicts 0 vs 96 (FCFS) and 0 (rule-based).
Fairness (Jain): 0.805 vs 0.754 (FCFS) and 0.798 (rule-based); urgent requests held 57.3% vs 45.0% and 54.4%.

Weakest metric for the intelligent method: Average waiting time (-1.9% vs rule-based, worse). Most of the gain over FCFS comes from respecting the class timetable and flexible meeting lengths (already present in rule-based); the scoring layer adds smaller gains. Data are synthetic.
